newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Reps challenge school funding cut in budget.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Reps challenge school funding cut in budget.

text.p: More than 100 U.S. House members called on President Clinton and key House and Senate leaders on Wednesday to rethink a decision not to include $5 billion in school construction funding in the new balanced budget pact.

Reps. Harold Ford, D-Tenn.; Nita Lowey, D-N.Y., Peter Deutsch, D-Fla., and dozens more said in letters to Clinton and others that they feel "deep concern" that the funding -- which Clinton himself had proposed in March -- did not make it into the two-week-old agreement.

"We appreciate the delicate balance reached between the Administration and Republican leadership on elements of the budget agreement," said the roughly 104 signers, all but about two of which are Democrats.

"Nevertheless, we stand firm in our belief that $5 billion in funding for school construction must be a central component of any final budget proposal because the need for these resources is critical," the signers said.

In addition to Clinton, the letters went to Rep. Bob Livingston, R-La., chair of the House Appropriations Committee; Rep. John Kasich, R-Ohio, chair of the House Budget Committee ; Rep. Bill Archer, R-Texas, chair of the House Ways and Means Committee, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, R-Miss., and Sen. Pete Domenici, R-N.M., chair of the Senate Budget Committee.

The school construction measure was originally included in the President's fiscal 1998 proposed budget, but it was dropped two weeks ago during the negotiations between the White House and GOP leaders.
Rep. Nita Lowey, D-N.Y., has introduced legislation embodying the plan.

The bill, which has 96 cosponsors, would allocate $5 billion in federal funds nationwide for school infrastructure repair, construction and improvements. About $2.45 billion would go directly to the largest 100 U.S. school districts and another $2.45 billion would be distributed to the 50 states.
"This budget deal cheats our students and shortchanges our schools," Lowey said at a press briefing on Wednesday. "I am outraged that this critical proposal was dropped from the budget."

Rep. Ford, whose congressional district would get roughly $20 million to leverage capital construction projects under the bill, said, "This sends a pretty awesome signal to our children ... and to my district."
Ford said there is room for change in the budget. "This agreement hasn't been voted on at all," he said of the new pact. "I'm hopeful we'll be able to work this out now that it's coming to Congress."
Ford said the letter went to Lott because the senator urged Clinton to take the construction funding out of the draft budget agreement.
The new joint budget pact does call for some increases in education spending, such as a hike in Head Start funds.
